Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We investigate the evolution of binary fractions in star clusters using N-body models of up to 100000 stars. Primordial binary frequencies in these models range from 5% to 50%. Simulations are performed with the NBODY4 code and include a full mass spectrum of stars, stellar evolution, binary evolution and the tidal field of the Galaxy. We find that the overall binary fraction of a cluster almost always remains close to the primordial value, except at late times when a cluster is near dissolution. A critical exception occurs in the central regions where we observe a marked increase in binary fraction with time -- a simulation starting with 100000 stars and 5% binaries reached a core binary frequency as high as 40% at the end of the core-collapse phase (occurring at 16 Gyr with ~20000 stars remaining). Binaries are destroyed in the core by a variety of processes as a cluster evolves, but the combination of mass-segregation and creation of new binaries in exchange interactions produces the observed increase in relative number. We also find that binaries are cycled into and out of cluster cores in a manner that is analogous to convection in stars. For models of 100000 stars we show that the evolution of the core-radius up to the end of the initial phase of core-collapse is not affected by the exact value of the primordial binary frequency (for frequencies of 10% or less). We discuss the ramifications of our results for the likely primordial binary content of globular clusters.

# The Evolution of Binary Fractions in Star Clusters: Insights from N-Body Simulations

## Simulation Methodology

This study employs sophisticated N-body models comprising up to 100,000 stars to investigate the complex dynamics of binary star fraction evolution within star clusters. The simulations utilize the NBODY4 code, a well-established computational framework capable of capturing the intricate physics governing dense stellar systems. Critically, these models incorporate several essential physical ingredients that contribute to realistic cluster evolution: a full stellar mass spectrum representing realistic initial mass functions, detailed stellar evolution algorithms that track how individual stars change over cosmic timescales, binary evolution processes that account for the complex interactions between paired stars, and the Galactic tidal field, which governs the external gravitational influences that gradually strip stars from the cluster and drive its long-term dissolution.

## Global Binary Fraction Stability

One of the key findings from these simulations concerns the overall binary fraction of the cluster as a whole. Throughout the majority of a cluster's evolutionary history, this global binary fraction remains remarkably close to its primordial (initial) value. This stability persists across most of the cluster's lifetime, suggesting that the bulk population of binaries in the outer regions and halo of the cluster is relatively unaffected by the dynamical processes occurring in the denser central regions. Only during the very late stages of cluster evolution—as the system approaches complete dissolution—does this global binary fraction begin to deviate significantly from its initial value, reflecting the increasingly dominant influence of tidal stripping and the preferential loss of single stars relative to more massive binary systems.

## Dramatic Central Concentration of Binaries

In stark contrast to the stability observed in the global binary fraction, the central regions of the cluster tell a dramatically different story. The core binary fraction exhibits substantial growth over time, demonstrating the profound impact of dynamical processes concentrated in the cluster's densest regions. In one representative model, a cluster beginning with a modest 5% primordial binary fraction experiences remarkable growth in its central binary population. By the time the cluster reaches core-collapse—occurring at approximately 16 Gyr—the core binary frequency has increased dramatically to as much as 40%. This represents nearly an order-of-magnitude enhancement in the concentration of binaries within the cluster's central regions compared to the primordial population.

## Physical Mechanisms Driving Core Enrichment

This substantial increase in core binary fraction arises from the interplay of multiple physical processes operating simultaneously within the cluster core. Mass segregation plays a fundamental role in this enrichment: because binary systems are effectively more massive than single stars, they experience enhanced dynamical friction and sink preferentially toward the cluster center through two-body relaxation processes. This segregation effect naturally concentrates existing binaries in the core over time.

Simultaneously, the formation of new binaries through exchange interactions contributes significantly to core binary enrichment. In the dense stellar environment of the cluster core, three-body and higher-order encounters frequently result in exchange interactions where single stars swap into existing binary systems, replacing one of the original binary components. These exchange processes effectively convert single stars into binary members, further boosting the local binary fraction.

Importantly, this net increase in core binary fraction occurs despite the continuous operation of binary destruction processes within the same dense central environment. Close encounters between binaries and single stars, or between multiple binaries, can lead to binary disruption, ionization, or merger events that remove binaries from the population. The observed net growth in core binary fraction thus represents the outcome of a delicate balance between binary formation and destruction mechanisms, with formation processes ultimately winning out over the destruction channels during the evolutionary phases leading up to core-collapse.

## The Convective Cycling Process

A particularly illuminating aspect of this research reveals that binaries undergo continuous cycling into and out of the cluster core throughout the evolutionary process. This phenomenon bears a striking analogy to convective processes observed in stellar interiors, where material circulates between different regions in a dynamic, ongoing exchange. In the cluster context, binaries are dynamically processed within the core—potentially undergoing hardening through encounters, participating in exchange interactions, or experiencing various dynamical modifications—before being ejected back into the outer regions of the cluster through the recoil from energetic encounters. This continuous circulation ensures that the core binary population remains dynamically active and constantly renewed, rather than representing a static reservoir of primordial binaries.

Furthermore, the research demonstrates an important robustness in the cluster's structural evolution: the evolution of the core radius leading up to core-collapse remains remarkably insensitive to the primordial binary frequency, provided this initial fraction is 10% or lower. This finding suggests that while binaries play a crucial role in the later dynamical evolution of the cluster core (including potentially providing the energy source that halts core-collapse), their presence at these modest primordial levels does not significantly alter the fundamental timescale or pattern of core contraction that characterizes the cluster's approach to core-collapse.

# The Evolution of Binary Star Populations in Star Clusters: An N-Body Study

## Introduction

Binary stars are fundamental building blocks of star clusters, playing a crucial role in shaping their dynamical evolution, energy production, and eventual dissolution. Despite decades of observational and theoretical work, the primordial binary fraction of globular clusters—the fraction of stars that formed in binary systems before any dynamical processing occurred—remains one of the most poorly constrained parameters in cluster formation theory. Understanding how binary populations evolve from their initial conditions to their present-day configurations is essential not only for interpreting current observations of binary fractions in globular clusters, but also for constraining star formation processes in dense stellar environments.

This study addresses this problem through a comprehensive suite of direct N-body simulations designed to track the long-term evolution of binary star populations in star clusters. By systematically varying the initial binary fraction and following clusters through essentially their entire evolutionary history—from initial relaxation through core collapse and toward eventual dissolution—we aim to disentangle the complex interplay between stellar evolution, binary star evolution, internal dynamical processes, and external tidal effects that collectively determine the binary content observed in real clusters today.

## Methodology

### Numerical Approach

We employ the direct N-body integration code NBODY4, which utilizes the Ahmad-Cohen neighbor scheme combined with special-purpose GRAPE hardware to achieve the computational efficiency necessary for modeling realistic star cluster populations. Unlike Monte Carlo or Fokker-Planck approaches, direct N-body integration follows the individual gravitational interactions of every star in the simulation, providing an accurate treatment of the close encounters, binary formation, and exchange interactions that are critical to binary star dynamics but difficult to capture in more approximate methods.

Our simulations include star cluster models ranging up to N = 100,000 stars, representing some of the largest direct N-body simulations of binary-rich clusters performed to date. This range of cluster sizes allows us to examine how binary evolution depends on the total number of stars, and by extension, on the relaxation timescale of the system.

### Physical Ingredients

The simulations incorporate several physical processes essential for realistic cluster modeling:

1. **Stellar evolution**: Individual stars evolve according to standard stellar evolution prescriptions, including main-sequence evolution, post-main-sequence phases, and the production of stellar remnants (white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes). This is critical because stellar evolution affects both the masses of cluster members and the internal evolution of binary systems.

2. **Binary star evolution**: Binaries in our simulations undergo their own internal evolution, including mass transfer, common envelope evolution, and other processes that can alter binary orbital parameters or lead to stellar mergers. This coupling between stellar and binary evolution is essential for accurately tracking how binary populations change over time.

3. **Galactic tidal field**: Each cluster model is embedded within an external tidal field representative of the Galactic potential, allowing for the gradual removal of stars from the outer regions of the cluster and enabling us to track cluster evolution through to near-dissolution in some models.

### Initial Conditions

We explore a range of primordial binary fractions from 5% to 50%, spanning the range suggested by various observational and theoretical considerations for the initial conditions of globular clusters. This range allows us to test whether the evolutionary pathways of binary populations depend sensitively on the initial binary content, and to identify observational diagnostics that might help discriminate between different primordial binary fractions.

## Results

### Global Binary Fraction Evolution

Perhaps the most striking result of our simulations is the remarkable stability of the overall (global) binary fraction throughout most of a cluster's evolutionary history. Despite the cluster losing significant numbers of single stars to tidal stripping and evaporation over many relaxation times, the total binary fraction integrated over the entire cluster remains close to its primordial value for an extended period. Only as the cluster approaches final dissolution does the global binary fraction begin to show significant deviations from its initial value, primarily because binaries—being more massive on average than single stars—are preferentially retained as the cluster loses mass, while soft binaries can also be destroyed by the tidal field or through dynamical encounters near the tidal boundary.

This finding has important implications for observational studies: measurements of the global binary fraction in present-day globular clusters may provide a reasonably direct constraint on the primordial binary fraction, provided the cluster has not yet reached an advanced state of dissolution.

### Core Binary Fraction Evolution

In stark contrast to the stability of the global binary fraction, we find that the binary fraction within the cluster core evolves dramatically over time. Binaries, being more massive on average than the typical single star in the cluster, undergo mass segregation and sink toward the cluster core on a timescale related to the local relaxation time. This process concentrates binaries in the central regions well before the cluster reaches core collapse.

In our simulations, we observe core binary fractions that increase from initial values as low as 5% up to 40% or higher by the time of core collapse. This dramatic enhancement occurs through two complementary mechanisms:

1. **Mass segregation**: Binaries, having higher total mass than single stars, migrate toward the cluster core through two-body relaxation processes, becoming increasingly concentrated in the central regions as the cluster evolves.

2. **Exchange interactions**: Dynamical encounters between single stars and existing binaries in the dense core frequently result in exchange interactions, where a single star replaces one component of the binary. Because these interactions preferentially retain more massive stars in binary systems, and because such interactions preferentially occur in the dense core, they contribute further to the buildup of the core binary population.

### The Binary "Convection" Cycle

Perhaps the most novel aspect of our results is the identification of what we term a "convection-like" cycling of binary stars through the cluster core. Rather than being a static, ever-growing reservoir of binaries, the core binary population undergoes continuous processing:

- Binaries sink into the core through mass segregation
- Within the dense core environment, binaries undergo dynamical interactions—being hardened (their orbits shrink) through encounters with passing stars, exchanging components, or occasionally being ionized (destroyed) through strong encounters
- Hardened binaries, through the encounters that harden them, receive kinetic energy kicks that can eject them from the core into the outer regions of the cluster
- These ejected binaries slowly resettle through relaxation processes, eventually re-entering the core to repeat the cycle

This cyclical process means that the core is not simply accumulating a passive population of primordial binaries, but is instead actively processing binaries through repeated episodes of dynamical interaction, redistributing energy throughout the cluster in a manner reminiscent of convective heat transport in stellar interiors. This cycling has important consequences for the energy budget of the cluster and for the properties of the binaries themselves, as repeated hardening and exchange interactions modify orbital periods, eccentricities, and component masses over time.

## Discussion and Implications

Our results provide several important constraints and insights for understanding binary populations in real globular clusters:

**Constraining primordial binary fractions**: The dramatic difference between the evolution of global and core binary fractions suggests that the choice of observational aperture matters enormously when comparing simulations to observations. Studies that measure binary fractions only in cluster cores may substantially overestimate the primordial binary fraction if dynamical evolution effects are not properly accounted for. Conversely, global binary fraction measurements, when available, may provide more direct constraints on primordial conditions.

**Core collapse dynamics**: The buildup of binaries in the core through mass segregation directly influences the timing and nature of core collapse. Binaries provide an energy source that can halt or reverse core collapse through binary "burning" (the release of orbital energy during hardening encounters), meaning that the primordial binary fraction has significant consequences for the overall dynamical history of the cluster, including the timing of core collapse and the character of post-collapse oscillations.

**Population diversity across cluster mass**: Our simulations spanning N = 1,000 to 100,000 stars reveal that the details of binary processing depend on cluster size, with the relaxation timescale setting the pace at which mass segregation and the associated core binary buildup occur. This suggests that binary fraction observations should be interpreted in the context of a cluster's specific dynamical age and relaxation time, rather than assuming a universal evolutionary track.

## Conclusions

This comprehensive suite of N-body simulations demonstrates that binary star populations in globular clusters undergo complex, spatially-dependent evolution driven by the combined effects of stellar evolution, binary evolution, internal dynamics, and external tidal fields. While global binary fractions remain remarkably stable and close to primordial values for most of a cluster's lifetime, core binary fractions increase dramatically due to mass segregation and exchange interactions, revealing a dynamic convection-like cycling of binaries through the dense central regions. These findings provide crucial guidance for interpreting observations of binary populations in real globular clusters and for constraining the primordial binary fractions that characterized the initial conditions of cluster formation.

# Primordial Simulations of Galaxy Formation

Understanding how galaxies emerged from the primordial universe represents one of the most compelling challenges in modern astrophysics. Computer simulations have become indispensable tools for reconstructing this cosmic history, allowing researchers to model the evolution of matter from the earliest moments after the Big Bang through to the complex galactic structures we observe today.

## The Primordial Universe as Starting Point

In the aftermath of the Big Bang, the universe was a nearly uniform soup of hot plasma, with only tiny density fluctuations—variations of roughly one part in a hundred thousand—imprinted during cosmic inflation. These minuscule primordial irregularities, later observed in the cosmic microwave background radiation, served as the seeds for all subsequent structure formation. Without these initial perturbations, gravity would have had nothing to amplify, and the universe would have remained essentially featureless.

## The Role of Simulations

Since analytical solutions to the equations governing structure formation quickly become intractable once nonlinear gravitational collapse begins, scientists rely on large-scale numerical simulations. These computational models track billions of particles representing dark matter and baryonic gas, evolving their positions and velocities according to the laws of gravity and hydrodynamics over billions of years of simulated time.

Prominent simulation projects—such as Illustris, EAGLE, and IllustrisTNG—have successfully reproduced many observed properties of galaxies, including their masses, sizes, and spatial distribution. These simulations begin with initial conditions derived directly from primordial density fields, essentially rewinding the observed cosmic microwave background fluctuations forward in time to watch structure emerge.

## From Dark Matter Halos to Galaxies

A critical insight from these simulations is the hierarchical nature of galaxy formation. Primordial density fluctuations first collapse into dark matter halos, which then act as gravitational wells that attract and compress gas. Within these halos, gas cools, condenses, and eventually ignites star formation, giving birth to the first galaxies. Simulations reveal that this process is not smooth or continuous but involves mergers, feedback from supernovae and active galactic nuclei, and complex interactions between dark matter and ordinary matter.

## Challenges and Future Directions

Despite remarkable successes, primordial simulations still face significant challenges. Resolving the full range of physical scales—from cosmological distances down to individual star-forming regions—requires enormous computational resources and clever approximations. Additionally, incorporating accurate models of feedback processes, which regulate star formation and shape galactic properties, remains an active area of research.

As computational power grows and observational data from instruments like the James Webb Space Telescope provides new constraints on early galaxies, simulations of the primordial universe will continue to refine our understanding of how the first structures in the cosmos gave rise to the diverse galaxies that populate it today.

# Abstract

We investigate the dynamical evolution of binary star fractions in globular clusters using a suite of direct N-body simulations performed with the NBODY4 code. Binary stars play a crucial role in the long-term structural and dynamical evolution of star clusters, acting as an internal energy source that can delay or prevent core collapse. However, the processes governing the depletion and survival of binary populations across a cluster's lifetime remain incompletely understood. We model star clusters with a range of initial conditions, including varying initial binary fractions (5%-30%), primordial mass segregation, King concentration parameters, and total particle numbers (N = 10^4 - 10^5), to isolate the dominant mechanisms driving binary fraction evolution. Our simulations self-consistently include stellar evolution, tidal stripping from the Galactic potential, and binary-single and binary-binary encounters that lead to hardening, softening, and ionization of binaries.

We find that the binary fraction evolves non-monotonically over a Hubble time, with an initial rapid decline driven by the ionization of soft binaries and stellar evolution mass loss, followed by a slower, quasi-steady decline as the cluster approaches and passes through core collapse. Dynamical processing preferentially destroys low-binding-energy binaries while hardening tighter binaries, leading to a global increase in the average binding energy of surviving binaries even as their overall number decreases. We show that mass segregation causes binaries to sink into the cluster core early in the evolution, where they dominate the local density and drive core energy production, resulting in a pronounced central concentration of the binary population relative to single stars. The central binary fraction can be a factor of several higher than the global value at late times, with the discrepancy increasing as the cluster evolves toward and through core collapse. We quantify how the total binary fraction and its radial distribution depend on initial cluster concentration and particle number, finding that lower-concentration and lower-N clusters lose binaries more rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and weaker gravitational focusing in binary-single interactions. We compare our results to observed present-day binary fractions in Galactic globular clusters and demonstrate that our simulations can reproduce the observed anti-correlation between binary fraction and cluster central density, supporting the interpretation that dynamical processing is the primary regulator of binary populations in old, dense stellar systems. These results have implications for using binary fractions as diagnostic tools for the dynamical age and evolutionary history of globular clusters.

# The Evolution of Primordial Binary Populations in Star Clusters: Effects of Core Collapse and Mass Segregation

**Abstract**

We review and synthesize the theoretical and observational understanding of primordial binary star evolution within dense stellar clusters, focusing on the interplay between binary populations, mass segregation, and core collapse dynamics. Binary stars, present in significant fractions (20-100%) at cluster formation, serve as critical energy reservoirs that regulate cluster dynamical evolution through the Heggie-Hills mechanism, wherein hard binaries harden via superelastic encounters while soft binaries soften and disrupt. N-body simulations and Monte Carlo/Fokker-Planck models demonstrate that binaries, being systematically more massive than the mean stellar mass, undergo efficient dynamical mass segregation on timescales shorter than the half-mass relaxation time, concentrating preferentially within the cluster core. This segregation is further amplified by binary formation and hardening processes that occur most efficiently in the high-density core environment.

The presence of even a modest primordial binary fraction (f_b ~ 5-10%) fundamentally alters the classical core-collapse paradigm: binaries act as an internal heating source that can halt, delay, or entirely prevent deep core collapse by injecting orbital binding energy into the surrounding single-star population through three- and four-body encounters. This energy generation supports the core against contraction, driving clusters into long-lived, binary-burning quasi-equilibrium states analogous to stellar main-sequence evolution, before eventual transition to gravothermal oscillations once the binary reservoir is depleted. The core collapse timescale, its depth, and post-collapse oscillatory behavior are shown to depend sensitively on the initial binary fraction, binary orbital period distribution, and mass ratio distribution, with N_b/N ratios exceeding a few percent sufficient to suppress collapse over a Hubble time for realistic cluster masses.

We further discuss how binary-single and binary-binary interactions in the segregated core drive dynamical binary hardening, ejection of energetic binaries and merger products (including blue stragglers, compact object binaries, and hypervelocity stars), and exchange interactions that preferentially insert massive stars and compact remnants into binaries. These processes establish observable signatures—including the radial distribution of binaries, mass function variations with clustercentric distance, and the incidence of exotic binary populations—that provide empirical diagnostics of a cluster's dynamical age and initial binary content. We conclude by highlighting outstanding challenges in reconciling primordial binary statistics inferred from young clusters with those observed in dynamically evolved old globular clusters, and the implications for binary black hole formation channels in dense stellar environments.

# Abstract

We present a suite of direct N-body simulations of star clusters containing up to N = 100,000 stars, designed to investigate the coupled evolution of primordial binary populations and cluster dynamical structure over cosmologically relevant timescales. Using the NBODY6/NBODY7-class integration scheme with post-Newtonian corrections, individual stellar evolution, and full treatment of binary formation, hardening, and disruption channels, we follow the evolution of clusters with initial binary fractions ranging from 5% to 100%, initial concentrations spanning King W₀ = 3–9, and varying primordial mass segregation.

Our simulations demonstrate that binary fraction evolution is strongly coupled to the cluster's core dynamical state through a self-regulating feedback mechanism: binary-single and binary-binary encounters in the core generate dynamical heating that governs the timing and depth of core collapse, while the resulting density fluctuations modulate binary ionization and hardening rates. We find that the global binary fraction depletes on a timescale that scales with the initial half-mass relaxation time, with preferential destruction of soft binaries (a > a_hard) occurring within the first few relaxation times, followed by a slower depletion phase dominated by exchange interactions and dynamical burning of hard binaries in the post-collapse core.

Core binary fractions are found to exceed the global cluster value by factors of 2–10, consistent with mass segregation driving binaries—which are preferentially more massive than single stars—toward the cluster center. We quantify the resulting binary burning luminosity and its role in staving off deep core collapse, finding that clusters with initial binary fractions above ~20% experience significantly delayed and shallower core collapse compared to binary-free control runs, with implications for the observed diversity of core radii in Galactic globular clusters.

Comparing our simulated present-day binary fractions and radial distributions to Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based photometric surveys of Galactic globular clusters (including 47 Tuc, NGC 6752, and M4), we find good agreement when initial binary fractions of 10–30% are assumed, consistent with independent estimates from young star clusters and star-forming regions. Our results support the interpretation that present-day binary fractions in old globular clusters primarily reflect dynamical processing of a substantial primordial binary population rather than in-situ formation, and provide predictions for the binary radial distribution and core binary content as diagnostics of cluster dynamical age and initial conditions for upcoming deep photometric and spectroscopic surveys.

# Abstract

We present a systematic investigation into the role of primordial binary populations in shaping the dynamical evolution of dense star clusters, with particular emphasis on the binary fraction within the cluster core during and after core collapse. Using the direct N-body integration code NBODY4, incorporating realistic prescriptions for single and binary stellar evolution, we perform a suite of simulations of star clusters with initial binary frequencies ranging from 5% to 50%. Our models include a full treatment of stellar winds, supernova kicks, and binary interaction processes such as tidal circularization, mass transfer, and common envelope evolution, allowing us to capture the interplay between stellar and dynamical evolution in a self-consistent manner.

We find that the initial binary fraction plays a critical role in determining both the timing and depth of core collapse, as well as the subsequent evolution of the core binary fraction. Clusters with higher initial binary fractions experience delayed core collapse due to enhanced binary heating, which counteracts the gravothermal contraction of the core. Conversely, low initial binary fraction clusters undergo more rapid and pronounced core collapse, followed by a steep rise in the core binary fraction as dynamical processes preferentially destroy single stars through exchange interactions and ejections, while hardening surviving binaries. We quantify the dependence of the core binary fraction at the epoch of deepest core collapse on the initial binary frequency, revealing a non-monotonic relationship: intermediate initial binary fractions (~10-20%) yield the highest degree of core binary enhancement relative to their initial values, while very high initial fractions saturate the core binary population and suppress further dynamical amplification due to binary-binary interactions and reduced central density contrast.

We further examine the properties of binaries that survive to the core-collapse phase, finding that hard binaries with short orbital periods are preferentially retained and undergo significant hardening via three-body encounters, while soft binaries are efficiently disrupted. The resulting core binary fraction and orbital parameter distributions show clear dependence on the initial binary frequency, with implications for the interpretation of observed binary fractions in the cores of globular clusters. Our results demonstrate that primordial binary populations exert a controlling influence on both the global dynamical clock of star clusters and the detailed structure of their collapsed cores, providing crucial constraints for reconciling N-body models with observational binary fraction estimates in Galactic globular clusters. These findings underscore the necessity of realistic binary populations in N-body simulations aimed at understanding the long-term dynamical evolution of dense stellar systems.

# Binary Star Dynamics in Globular Clusters: Formation, Destruction, and Radial Redistribution

## Abstract

Binary stars play a fundamental role in shaping the long-term dynamical evolution of globular clusters, serving as both energy reservoirs and diagnostic tracers of cluster history. This work examines the competing processes that govern binary populations across a cluster's lifetime: primordial binaries inherited from star formation, dynamically formed binaries created through three-body encounters and tidal capture in dense stellar environments, and the destructive mechanisms—including ionizing encounters, exchange interactions, and stellar evolution effects—that deplete the binary fraction over time.

Central to this evolution is mass segregation, whereby binaries, being statistically more massive than single stars, sink toward the cluster core through dynamical friction on timescales shorter than the cluster's relaxation time. Once concentrated in the core, binaries participate preferentially in strong gravitational encounters, acting as an energy source that can temporarily halt or reverse core collapse (binary "burning"). These interactions simultaneously harden surviving binaries while destroying softer pairs, and frequently eject processed binaries and single stars into the cluster's outer regions or beyond the tidal radius entirely.

We synthesize evidence from N-body simulations and observational surveys demonstrating that the radial distribution of binaries evolves substantially over a Hubble time: initially uniform or centrally concentrated populations become increasingly segregated, with the core binary fraction reflecting a dynamic equilibrium between segregation inflow, burning/ejection outflow, and destruction. The outer cluster regions, by contrast, retain a more primordial, dynamically unprocessed binary population less affected by close encounters. This radial dichotomy in binary properties—fraction, period distribution, and eccentricity—provides a powerful observational probe of a cluster's dynamical age and its integrated encounter history, with direct implications for the production of exotic binary products (blue stragglers, X-ray binaries, millisecond pulsars) preferentially found in cluster cores.

**Keywords:** globular clusters, binary stars, stellar dynamics, mass segregation, core collapse, N-body simulations
